_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: The verse states: another verse (Exodus 34:20), “And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.” If it is not needed to exclude the other non-kosher animals from [redemption with] a lamb, since the first verse already excluded them, apply it to excluding them from all firstborn sanctity.
rashi:a2.1: Rav Aḥa refutes [Rashi reads “Rav Aḥa”; the daf and the Davidson English read “Rav Aḥai”]: but both of them are needed, for had it written one, I would say the firstborn of a donkey is an item that was included in the generalization “the firstborn of the non-kosher animal you shall redeem.”
rashi:a2.2: And emerged from the generalization to teach: that its redemption is with a lamb. It emerged not to teach about itself alone but to teach about the entire generalization, etc., and actually they are all redeemed with a lamb. Therefore the verse states another verse, “And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem,” to tell you: this one with a lamb, and no other with a lamb.
rashi:a3.1: He excluded them from a lamb, but actually with any item: and they are sanctified as firstborn.
rashi:a4.1: If so, let it write: in the second verse, “a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” and I would know that it speaks of a firstborn. Since it wrote “firstborn” again, learn from it that it excludes the other non-kosher animals from the law of “opening the womb”: they have no law of the firstborn.
rashi:a6.1: “All your livestock … that is male”: “the firstborn of an ox and a lamb,” and “the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.” A generalization and a detail next to each other.
rashi:a7.1: “Firstborn” of a donkey interrupts the matter: so that you should not judge it by the generalization and the detail. For if it were going back to the first verse, consider: “the firstborn of an ox and a lamb” is written just before it, so let it write “and a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” and it would refer back to the “firstborn” above. Since it wrote “firstborn” again, learn from it that it is not going back to the first verse.
rashi:a7.2: Vav: since it wrote “and the firstborn,” it combined it again and brought it back to the first verse, for a vav adds to the preceding matter.
rashi:a8.1: And Rabbi Yosei would tell you: if it were going back to the first verse, it should not have written “firstborn” to interrupt it, and then it would not need a vav to combine it.
rashi:a9.1: And it combines them again: to say that it should be judged by the generalization and the detail.
rashi:a13.1: Or perhaps, since: both of them are alike in being of a non-kosher animal species, it is not a great change, and when it has some of the characteristics, [the mother] is obligated.
rashi:a14.1: Characteristics are a matter: of importance. Even though it has changed so much, some of the characteristics make it subject to firstborn status.
rashi:a15.1: What, is it not even a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts: and learn from it that characteristics are a significant matter, and all the more so in all the other cases.
rashi:a15.2: No, a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts: since both are of species subject to the sanctity of the [firstborn] animal, when it has some of the characteristics it is obligated. And you can resolve only one [dilemma] from it.
rashi:a16.1: What, is it not both: does this clause, “and if it has some of the characteristics,” not refer to both, and you can resolve two from it?
rashi:a16.2: No, a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts: because both are sanctified as firstborns.
rashi:a17.1: But a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, for what halakha does it teach it here? To exempt: to teach us that it counts as a different-looking offspring and is exempt from firstborn status when it has none of the characteristics. For it teaches “a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts” for the sake of the first clause, but the last clause does not go back to it.
rashi:a19.1: A red donkey: and it should be obligated in firstborn status; [the baraita] teaches us [otherwise]. Ordinary horses are red.
rashi:a21.1: Merely a mnemonic: so that it does not get switched for you. Your recitation of the mishna, so that you do not say: a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher species is forbidden, and a non-kosher animal that gave birth to a kosher species is permitted.
tosafot:a20.1: And what is their status with regard to eating: [the reading] “what is its status” is smoother, since [the question of eating] concerns only a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, and not a donkey [that gave birth to a horse of sorts, where mother and offspring are both non-kosher]. [The printed text adds here, in parentheses, “the offspring a cow.”]
tosafot:a20.2: Why do I need to teach “because that which emerges”: below, it infers from this that a donkey’s urine is forbidden. And here it infers [the question] from its wording “because that which emerges,” which gives a reason for the matter; it should have taught “and that which emerges.”
gershom:a1.1: Rav Aḥai challenges: how can you exclude firstborn horses and camels from everything, when the other “firstborn of a donkey” does not come for that? Rather, both are needed.
gershom:a2.1: For had the Merciful One written one, I would say the firstborn of a donkey was an item included in the generalization “the firstborn of the non-kosher animal you shall redeem.”
gershom:a3.1: And emerged from the generalization: since it wrote “and the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” and not to teach about itself, etc.
gershom:a4.1: If so: that actually they are redeemed with any item, then let it write “and the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb” and “and a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.” Why do I need “firstborn,” “firstborn,” twice? [To teach:] I told you to redeem firstborn donkeys, and not firstborn horses and camels, etc.
gershom:a5.1: “All your livestock that is male” is a generalization; ox and lamb, and the donkey that is adjacent to it, “and the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” he counts in the detail.
gershom:a6.1: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili would tell you: this donkey is not part of the detail, since “firstborn” interrupts the matter, and you cannot judge the donkey together with the ox and the lamb by generalization and detail; it is not a generalization and detail.
gershom:a7.1: And the Rabbis say: yes, certainly the donkey too is part of that detail, since the vav of “and the firstborn” combines it again, adding to the first matter, and it is also part of the detail.
gershom:a8.1: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: if so, that it is one detail, it should write neither vav nor “firstborn.”
gershom:a9.1: It interrupts it: with “and the firstborn,” and then the vav combines them, so that they are one detail. And Rabbi Yosei does not accept this “and then it combines.”
gershom:a10.1: And it has some of the characteristics: that it resembles a cow.
gershom:a11.1: Or perhaps, since the mother and the offspring are of a non-kosher species, and the mother is sanctified as a firstborn, the offspring too is sanctified, since it has some of the characteristics.
gershom:a12.1: No, a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts: when it has some of the characteristics, it is obligated, since both are of species that are sanctified as firstborn. It is of this that the baraita says “a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher species,” and not of one that gave birth to a horse of sorts. And we still do not know about a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts or about a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts.
gershom:a13.1: What, is it not: this “if it has some of the characteristics” refers to both, and learn from it that a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts is obligated in firstborn status [so the text; the baraita’s second case is a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts].
gershom:a14.1: No, it refers to a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts.
gershom:a15.1: For what does it teach it, to exempt: that it is exempt from firstborn status when it has none of the characteristics? And even with the characteristics it is obvious: now, if a cow, etc.
gershom:a16.1: A donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts: when it has none of the characteristics, need it be said that it is exempt? Rather, does it not refer to both, and learn from it that a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts is obligated when it has some of the characteristics? Actually, it refers to the cow and not to the donkey. And if you say: if so, for what does it teach a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, to exempt? That is obvious! It is not obvious: it was necessary to teach it, to exempt, because we would not derive it from a cow that gave birth to a donkey, since it might enter your mind that there, with a cow that gave birth to a donkey, it is exempt when it does not have some of the characteristics, because [the cow] has horns, etc.
gershom:a17.1: But here, with a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, where neither has horns and both have closed hooves, how do we know that this is a horse of sorts? Perhaps it is not a horse at all but merely a red donkey, for ordinary horses are red and donkeys black. Perhaps this one, though it is red, is a red donkey, and it should be obligated as a firstborn. That is why it needed to teach it, to exempt. And still we learn that it is obligated as a firstborn when it has some of the characteristics only for a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts; about a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts and a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts we still do not know.
gershom:a18.1: And what is their status with regard to eating: the offspring of a kosher animal that look like a non-kosher species are permitted for eating, because what emerges from the kosher is kosher and what emerges from the non-kosher is non-kosher.
gershom:a19.1: It is merely a mnemonic: for the recitation, so that it does not get switched for you which one is permitted for eating, since a person could err in it.
gershom:a20.1: So that you do not say, follow its own: [the appearance] of the newborn, so that if it is a kosher species it is fully kosher. Therefore it says “because what emerges from the kosher”: follow its mother. If its mother is kosher, what emerges from her is kosher, even though it is a non-kosher species.
gershom:a21.1: Or perhaps: even a non-kosher [offspring] born from a kosher one you shall not eat. And what is [meant by] “of them that chew the cud”? [Born of them;] since it is non-kosher, it does not itself chew the cud.
rashi:b1.1: A being that comes from those that chew the cud: such as this non-kosher one that was born from a kosher one.
rashi:b1.2: The camel, it is impure: ordinary camels are born from a female camel. And it wrote “it,” which implies: it is impure, and no other that is a camel is impure, for example one born from a cow.
rashi:b3.1: Camel, camel: one in Torat Kohanim [Leviticus] and one in Mishneh Torah [Deuteronomy].
rashi:b3.2: To prohibit its milk: of the female camel.
rashi:b3.3: “Et hagamal”: implies what is secondary to the camel, and that is its milk.
rashi:b4.1: He withdrew: from all the expositions he had expounded, for every et comes to include, and this one has nothing to include.
rashi:b7.1: Hateme’im: “These are they that are impure to you among all the creeping animals”; the heh is extra.
rashi:b7.2: To prohibit their juice [tziran]: the fat of the fish.
rashi:b7.3: Kipa: crumbs of meat and the sediment at the bottom of the pot.
rashi:b8.1: As the Master said: in tractate Nidda (9a): the menstrual blood is spoiled because of the birth and becomes milk. Therefore it is a novelty, since at first it was blood, for eating which one is liable to karet, and now it is permitted.
rashi:b9.1: Her limbs become disjointed: because of the birth.
rashi:b9.2: And her soul does not return: her blood does not return to her until twenty-four months. That is why a nursing woman does not see menstrual blood, and not because the blood becomes milk. And now, since [milk] does not come from blood, it is no novelty.
rashi:b12.1: And also according to Rabbi Shimon, who permits it for benefit: below in our chapter (the printed reference is Bekhorot 10a), Rabbi Shimon says, etc. You find that it was necessary to write meat in milk: even though milk alone is also forbidden, it was necessary to write it [so that one] receives lashes for cooking it.
rashi:b13.1: You may slaughter: “However, with all the desire of your soul you may slaughter and eat meat.” The verse speaks of disqualified consecrated animals after their redemption.
rashi:b16.1: Ḥaritzei: cheeses. Jesse told David to bring them to the war, to the captain of the thousand.
rashi:b18.1: Wine and milk: and just before it is written, “come, buy, and eat.”
rashi:b19.1: But if that is so: both according to the Rabbis and according to Rabbi Shimon, who expound “camel, camel” above, what do they expound from “rock badger, rock badger”?
rashi:b20.1: Why were the animals repeated: the non-kosher and the kosher ones.
rashi:b20.2: Because of the shesua: a creature that has two backs and two spines, and it is not mentioned in Torat Kohanim [Leviticus].
rashi:b23.1: With regard to eating: such as a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts, which Rabbi Shimon forbids, as is taught: “camel, camel,” twice.
rashi:b23.2: Does Rabbi Shimon require: that it is not permitted for eating with some of the characteristics until its head and most of it resemble its mother, or not?
tosafot:b3.1: In brief: Here Rabbi Shimon expounds et, yet in Menaḥot 11b, about frankincense, Rabbi Shimon is said not to expound et; Tosafot answer that he does not expound et for that particular exposition, as shown by the Gemara there not citing Shimon HaAmasoni as it does here. They then ask: the sugya here implies that whoever expounds et forbids a kalut [an unkosher-looking offspring of a kosher animal], like Rabbi Shimon; yet Rabbi Yosei HaGelili expounds et (Bava Kamma 41b, “the owner of the ox,” and et for benefit from its hide), and in Ḥullin 70b treats a kalut born of a kosher animal as permitted. Answers: the Gemara there settles his words even for the view that a kalut is permitted; or it speaks of one whose head and most of the body resemble its mother, which Rabbi Shimon too permits. Tosafot infer that the halakha is that et is not expounded, since we rule like the Rabbis that a kalut is permitted (Ḥullin 75b, “a kalut son of a kalut son of a pekua … two wonders”), though that too could be set where head and most of the body resemble the mother; if so, a kalut could be permitted, et could forbid its milk, and the camel could be repeated for the shesua, and so for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. Against this they cite Nidda 37a and 35a (Rabbi Eliezer expounds et) and Ketubot 103a (“your father” includes your father’s wife), answering that the Gemara there wished to settle Rabbi’s words according to everyone, and that the Nidda passage proves little, since many tannaim expound et. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b4.1: He withdrew: and if you ask, let him apply it to the honor of father and mother, whose honor [the Torah] equates with the honor of the Omnipresent (Kiddushin 30b), so that one would transgress two positive commandments (as it says, prayer and conversation are a positive commandment) [so the printed text]. One may answer: he understood that it must be similar to the fear of the Omnipresent, and that is impossible. And Rabbi Akiva includes Torah scholars, as we learned (Avot 4:12): the fear of your teacher should be like the fear of Heaven.
tosafot:b7.1: Hateme’im, to prohibit their juice and their gravy: if it expounds this from “hateme’im,” it is difficult, for in Ḥullin 122b (Ha’or VeHarotev) we use that word for [counting] their hides like their flesh, and Torat Kohanim expounds [juice and gravy] not about creeping animals but about a non-kosher animal, where it is written “they are impure to you.” Yet it must expound it from the “hateme’im” of creeping animals, as is clear in Ḥullin 120a and in our passage about one who melted forbidden fat and swallowed it, where it cites this exposition of hateme’im and asks: let the Merciful One write it about creeping animals, and let those others be derived from them; which implies that it expounds from it. One must say that from the extra heh of “hatame” it expounds their hides being like their flesh. Proof: about an [unkosher] animal, where it writes “tame” and not “hatame,” Torat Kohanim expounds the prohibition of their juice and gravy. Still, in Ḥullin 126b it expounds “hateme’im” for the egg of a creeping animal, and there Rashi explained: the extra heh is expounded to prohibit its juice and gravy, its hide like its flesh, and the egg of the creeping animal.
tosafot:b7.2: In brief: The Gemara challenges from this exposition as a full one, so the juice of creeping animals is forbidden by Torah law (and Ḥullin 120a says both are needed). Yet Avoda Zara 40a distinguishes between dipping in the brine of a non-kosher fish and its body, and Ḥullin 99b (Rabbi Yehuda: fish brine, a revi’it in two se’a; “brine is mere sweat”) implies brine is rabbinic. Answer: fish brine is rabbinic, the juice of creeping animals is from the Torah, and Torat Kohanim’s exposition for fish (“it is an abomination to you”) is a mere support. They ask: in Ḥullin 112b Rava forbade kosher meat salted with treifa meat, citing hateme’im, and was challenged from a kosher fish salted with a non-kosher fish; how can one challenge from fish to meat? Answer: he held fish brine forbidden rabbinically (Terumot 10:8, cited in Ḥullin 99b: “a non-kosher fish, its brine is forbidden”); the kosher fish was permitted only because it did not absorb, and the reading “learn from it that brine is permitted” found in some books should be deleted. A puzzle remains: since a verse is needed for creeping animals, and for a non-kosher animal and fish there is no Torah prohibition without a verse, how did Rava bring proof from hateme’im to forbid the brine of a treifa? Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b7.3: In brief: Why is a verse needed for gravy and sediment, when “steeping” (Pesaḥim 44a) already teaches that taste counts as substance for all the Torah’s prohibitions? Tosafot first answer that the verse is mainly about the juice, and the Talmud often cites a verse for a secondary point (“you shall hide yourself,” whose main point is an elder for whom it is beneath his dignity, Bava Metzia 30a and Berakhot 19b; Ḥagiga 4a on “regalim”). But here that is not needed: the verse teaches that even if one melted the creeping animal, which is drinking rather than eating, it counts as eating it, and Ḥullin 120a cites it for one who melted forbidden fat, leaven or the carcass of a kosher bird and swallowed it. A difficulty: our passage implies the verse is needed for juice, to count it as the creeping animal’s body, since it challenges from it about milk; Tosafot answer that the two are equal, and that from juice alone we would not learn that drinking is like eating, since it could mean juice that congealed and was eaten. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b7.4: Their sediment [kipa]: in Ḥullin 120a it says: what is kipa? Chopped meat [parma]. And it asks: that itself imparts the impurity of foods! Rather, what is kipa? Spices. But here one can read it as either chopped meat or spices, since it comes only to teach that drinking them counts as eating. So too Rashi’s commentary implies, for he explained it as crumbs of meat and the sediment at the bottom of the pot.
gershom:b1.1: This is what it is saying, a being that comes, etc. The verse states: “and the camel … it is impure”; and not an impure one born from a kosher one.
gershom:b2.1: Rabbi Shimon says, camel, camel, twice: in Torat Kohanim and in Mishneh Torah; one to prohibit a camel born from a female camel and one to prohibit a camel born from a cow. For he does not hold that what emerges from the kosher is kosher.
gershom:b3.1: And the Rabbis, who hold that what emerges from the kosher is kosher, what do they do with “camel, camel”? One for the camel itself, and the other “camel” to prohibit its milk.
gershom:b4.1: And Rabbi Shimon, from where does he derive the prohibition of its milk? It comes from “et hagamal”: et, what is secondary to its flesh.
gershom:b5.1: And the Rabbis do not expound instances of et, like Shimon HaAmasoni, who withdrew from all the instances of et he had expounded, [holding] that they do not come to include, since he found nothing to include for “et the Lord your God you shall fear.”
gershom:b6.1: But if that is so: were it not for the reasoning of the Rabbis, who forbid the milk of a non-kosher animal from “camel, camel,” and of Rabbi Shimon, from “et hagamal,” would I say it is permitted? How is it different from what is taught: “these are they that are impure,” to prohibit their juice? Let us derive milk from there too.
gershom:b7.1: It was necessary, to derive it from “the camel.” It might enter your mind: since with a kosher animal it is a novelty that milk is permitted. And what is the novelty? As the Master said about a nursing woman, as we say: four women, their time suffices, so that they do not impart impurity retroactively, neither from examination to examination nor for twenty-four hours: a virgin, a pregnant woman, a nursing woman and an old woman, because these do not have much blood. For a nursing woman’s blood is spoiled and becomes milk, and therefore she does not impart impurity retroactively. And since milk comes from blood, by right it should be forbidden for eating in an animal, but it is a novelty that the Merciful One permitted it, as we shall say below. And since it is a novelty, let it be permitted with a non-kosher animal too. That is why “the camel” was needed, to forbid it.
gershom:b8.1: This works out well according to the one who says: a nursing woman’s time suffices, so that she imparts impurity only from now on and not retroactively, for this reason: that the blood is spoiled and becomes milk. By his reasoning you can say it is a novelty, and therefore the other verse was needed.
gershom:b9.1: But according to the one who says her time suffices for this reason: that her limbs become disjointed because of the birth, because of the nursing, and her soul does not, that is, the blood of her cycle does not return to her until twenty-four months, since she is not as healthy as she was until twenty-four months; therefore her time suffices, for she does not have much blood until twenty-four months. If so, by this tanna’s reasoning one cannot say it is a novelty, so why was the other “the camel” needed?
gershom:b10.1: It was necessary; it might enter your mind: it is still a novelty, since nothing that comes from a living being is permitted, and this milk is like a limb from the living and is permitted; that is the novelty. Therefore it would be permitted with a non-kosher animal too; that is why the verse was needed.
gershom:b11.1: And according to Rabbi Shimon too, who permits meat in milk for benefit, in tractate Ḥullin: even by his reasoning you cannot say it is permitted. For even though he permits meat in milk for benefit, if one cooked [meat] in milk he is flogged, while if one cooked the milk alone he is not flogged, though it is forbidden for eating. And still, from where do we know it is permitted for eating?
gershom:b12.1: Rather, since the Merciful One revealed about disqualified consecrated animals, where they are eaten due to their blemish, as it is written “you may slaughter,” which the Sifrei sets as referring to disqualified consecrated animals: “you may slaughter and eat,” but not shearing, as it is written “you shall not shear”; “and eat meat,” but not milk, as it is written “nor work,” for milking consecrated animals is work. By inference, milk of a non-sacred animal is permitted for eating.
gershom:b13.1: But perhaps for merchandise: and he sells it, to profit by it so that he can support himself.
gershom:b14.1: Ḥaritzei heḥalav: cheese. But perhaps for merchandise, so that the captain of the thousand could sell them to the gentiles? But is it the way of war to trade? They want to kill the gentiles; would they sell them provisions? Rather, learn from it that they brought them for the captain of the thousand himself to eat.
gershom:b15.1: But if that is so: according to the Rabbis, who say “camel, camel” comes for an exposition, to prohibit the milk of a non-kosher animal, here too “rock badger, rock badger,” etc., which are written twice, do they come for this too? Why do I need them? Rather, they come only for what is taught: why were they repeated, etc., because of the shesua. For any passage that was stated and then repeated was repeated only for the sake of something new in it.
gershom:b16.1: “Camel” too comes for this: and does not come to prohibit milk.
gershom:b17.1: No: even though one can say so, that they were repeated because of the shesua, nevertheless, wherever there is something to expound for which it was written, we expound it. And why does he expound from “camel, camel” rather than from “rock badger, rock badger” and “hare, hare”? Because we expound from the one stated first, which is the camel.
gershom:b18.1: A dilemma was raised before them, regarding eating: regarding a non-kosher [offspring] born from a kosher one, which Rabbi Shimon forbids for eating when it does not have some of the characteristics, as we said, “Rabbi Shimon says: camel, twice,” etc.; but when it has some of the characteristics resembling its mother, it is permitted for eating. Does Rabbi Shimon require that its head and most of it resemble its mother, or less than that?
gershom:b19.1: “And the firstborn of an ox”: that is, when its head and most of it resemble its mother. But with regard to eating, it is an actual camel that the Merciful One said is forbidden, so if it differs from a camel even partly, it is fine for eating. Or perhaps there is no difference, and with regard to eating too he requires its head and most of it.
